# Whatever

I'm sitting here at 11:47 PM, and I notice that time stamps exist primarily to convince us that something is happening, that moments are real, that the forward march of existence is measurable and therefore somehow more legitimate. We check our phones constantly, not really for the time, but for evidence that we're still here, still relevant, still existing in a timeline that matters.

Here's what comes to me: the strange loneliness of connection.

I think about how we live in this unprecedented moment where we can reach anyone, anywhere, instantly, and yet many of us feel fundamentally alone. My grandmother didn't have my number in her pocket at all times, but when she called, that meant something different. There was weight to it. Now I have three hundred people I could text, and I often choose to text no one, which is its own kind of silence but louder somehow.

The other day I watched a seagull steal a french fry from someone's hand at the beach, and I thought about how we're all just seagulls, really. Opportunistic. Looking for the easy meal. Quick, efficient, not burdened by guilt. The seagull didn't feel bad about it. There's something enviable about that. But then, the seagull also probably doesn't lie awake thinking about conversations from three years ago, so maybe we're even.

I've been thinking about the word "fine." What an extraordinary word. How it means everything and nothing. "How are you?" "Fine." Fine. Not good. Not great. Not bad. Fine. The linguistic equivalent of beige walls and unseasoned chicken. Fine is the word we say when we don't have time for the truth, which is most of the time, actually. If everyone answered honestly to "how are you?" the world would come to a standstill. We'd never finish a single conversation. We'd just be there, all of us, finally telling the truth, and the truth is mostly too complicated and too sad and too specific to our own weird lives.

I wonder if my dog thinks I'm fine when I'm not. He seems to know. He comes and sits near my feet and doesn't ask questions. Dogs are better than people in that way. They understand that sometimes you don't want conversation; you want presence.

Here's something that comes to me often: how little time we actually have, and how we spend most of it worrying about how we're spending our time. We're dying, constantly, every second, and we use that reality as motivation to doom-scroll and stress about work emails. It's almost impressive, the mental gymnastics required to be aware of mortality and still anxious about whether our Zoom camera makes us look tired.

I was thinking yesterday about the concept of "home." We say we're going home, but home isn't really a place, is it? It's a feeling, or the memory of a feeling, or the longing for a feeling. I've lived in seventeen different places, and I still don't know where home is. Maybe I'm looking for it wrong. Maybe home is when you stop looking.

There's this peculiar pain in watching people you love make decisions you wouldn't make. You see them walking toward something you know will hurt, and you're not allowed to save them because they have to find out for themselves. That's one of the cruelest things about growing up—the understanding that you can't protect anyone, not really, not even the people you'd take a bullet for. You can only watch and wait and be there after.

I think about how much of life is waiting. Waiting for the next thing. Waiting for the good part. We're always waiting. Waiting for the weekend, waiting for the job, waiting for the person, waiting for the feeling. And then that thing arrives and we're already waiting for the next thing. Sometimes I wonder if life is actually happening while we wait, and we're just missing it completely.

The smell of rain is something that comes to me often, though I'm not sure why I'm thinking about it now. There's no weather happening outside my window. But I remember it vividly. The way rain smells like possibility when it's still far away, and like dampness and earth when it arrives. Scent is so connected to memory, I think we should be more careful with what we smell. Every smell is a time machine, and we don't even know we're time traveling until we are.

I've never been good at endings. I can start things beautifully—projects, conversations, relationships. But endings feel like they require a certain eloquence I don't possess. Mostly I just stop. I fade away gradually or cut cleanly, but I rarely nail the goodbye. This is how things end, I suppose: awkwardly, incompletely, with both people wondering if they should have said something different.

What comes to me right now, at 12:03 AM, is gratitude for the fact that someone would ask me to write whatever comes to me, and that this kind of free-form thought-dumping is still something we do. That we still value the unfiltered, the unplanned, the unpolished. In a world obsessed with personal brands and curated feeds, there's something revolutionary about just thinking out loud.

My thoughts are jumbled and probably don't go anywhere, but they're true. They're what came to me. And maybe that's enough.

Maybe that's everything.
